name: Tumbleweed
lede: Tumbleweed is a pale yellow classed in the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, named for the dried, rolling plant rather than any living green.

sections.title: A dried plant, not a green one
sections.body:
The 1955 ISCC-NBS system places Tumbleweed in block 89, a pale yellow, with Wikipedia as the library's other cited source and no record in Ridgway or Maerz and Paul [1]. The name describes the plant once it has dried, broken loose and rolled, bleached tan rather than green, which the warm, dusty hue reflects [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[peachbeige]] and [[pinkish-cinnamon]], at 
[[peach]], [[apricot]] and [[terracotta]] all turn up far more often than chance in paintings that also carry this color, alongside [[sienna]] and [[brick]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to Tumbleweed in 427 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.8 percent, as photographed [2]. It plays a highlight in 90 percent of its appearances, almost never a shadow [2]. Amedeo Modigliani, André Derain and Georges Seurat all use it well above the archive's average rate, with a 1710 stenciled scene of a lion and gazelle its strongest single match [2].

The earliest dated match is a Tibetan votive card from around 1000, nine and a half centuries before the ISCC-NBS classification, which only shows a similar screen color was photographed there, not that the name existed that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
